title: A DBS Tracker for Care Homes: Staff Documents and Expiry Dates in One Place
excerpt: An inspector asks to see a carer's right to work check. Here are the questions about staff documents that come up most, and how a single register with expiry alerts answers them.
meta_title: DBS Tracker for Care Homes: Keep Staff Documents in One Place
meta_description: Keep DBS, right to work, NMC and driving documents in one register with expiry alerts, so you can answer an inspector's staff file questions with the document in hand.
content:
"Show me the right to work check for the carer who joined eighteen months ago."

It is an ordinary request, and the manager knows the check was done. The question is where. The scan is in a shared drive, the original is in a lever arch file, and the visa end date is in the head of the person who is off this week.

A DBS tracker is the fix most services reach for first, and it is a good start. This post shows how to widen it. One register can hold the DBS, the right to work check, professional registration and the documents that only apply to some staff, with the file behind every entry and a warning before anything lapses. It is built around the questions inspectors tend to ask, because that is how a staff file really gets tested.

"Can I see the document, not the note?"

A spreadsheet that says "DBS checked" tells an inspector what you believe. The certificate tells them what is true.

Regulation 19 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 says persons employed for a regulated activity must be of good character, and that recruitment procedures must be operated effectively. It also says the information listed in Schedule 3 must be available for each person employed. That list includes proof of identity with a recent photograph, and, where required, the criminal record certificate.

So the document matters. On the CareStream workforce compliance register, every credential with an uploaded file has a View button. It opens the document in a window over the register, next to what you recorded: the reference number, issue and expiry dates, notes and status. You check the file against the entry without leaving the page, and you close the window and carry on down the list.

The View button only appears when a file has been uploaded. An entry with no file is plain to see, which is the point.

"When does this one run out?"

This is the question a DBS tracker exists to answer, and it is where paper and spreadsheets fail. Nobody opens them until something goes wrong.

The register colours each entry as valid, expiring or expired. Expiring means within 30 days. CareStream also sends admins a daily digest email of what is expiring or has expired, so the warning reaches you rather than waiting for you to look.

On DBS renewal, there is no single legal date, so the interval is your policy's decision. We cover the options in our guide on how often a DBS should be renewed. Whatever interval you choose, the register holds the date and nags you about it. Our safer recruitment and DBS policy shows the wording a service can adopt.

"Is their right to work still valid?"

A right to work check is not always a one off. For someone with a time limited right to work, the GOV.UK employer's guide describes follow up checks. The responsibility sits with the employer, and CareStream does not do the check or tell you the legal outcome. What it does is hold the document and the date, and warn you as the date approaches.

Two extras matter for services that recruit from overseas:

  • A visa entry can carry a sponsorship end date, for sponsored workers whose right to work has a time limit.
  • The daily digest covers it, including a visa whose sponsorship is ending.

These sit in an "Also held" column on the register. They are never marked as missing for staff they do not apply to. A British carer with no visa is not a red mark on your dashboard.

For the full picture of the check itself, see our post on the right to work check for employers.

"Are your nurses still registered?"

For a nursing home, the question that worries a manager most is whether every registered nurse's registration is current. Revalidation dates are easy to lose.

The register has a professional registration entry. You choose the body: the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC), the General Pharmaceutical Council (GPhC), the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC), the General Medical Council (GMC), Social Work England, or Other. You record the PIN or registration number, upload the certificate, and set the renewal or revalidation date. Then it behaves like any other credential: valid, expiring, expired.

One caution. The register holds what you enter. It does not look the person up on a professional register for you, so checking the register itself stays a manual task. What changes is that the date is no longer in someone's diary.

"What about the staff who drive?"

Home care services and some residential services have staff who drive for work. The register has optional entries for these, shown in the "Also held" column:

  • driving licence
  • business use insurance
  • MOT

They follow the same colours and the same 30 day warning, and they are never marked missing for staff who do not drive. There is also an entry for the employment contract, which you can read more about on the contract and holiday tab described below.

"Who is this person, and who do we call?"

The same register has a Personal details tab, visible to admins only: date of birth, emergency contact and next of kin, with a shortcut for "same as emergency contact". A Personal column shows how many of five sections are filled in, so gaps are visible at a glance.

A Contract and holiday tab holds the contract upload, contract type (permanent, fixed term, bank or zero hours), contracted hours, probation end date and holiday entitlement in days or hours. This is entitlement only. CareStream does not do holiday booking.

Staff pictures show next to each name on the register, which helps when a manager is looking down a long list of names that are only half familiar.

A short checklist for a quarterly look

  1. Open the register and look for expired and expiring entries.
  2. For each expired entry, find out whether the document has been renewed and the file not yet uploaded.
  3. Use View to check a sample of documents against what is recorded.
  4. Look at the "Also held" column for drivers and sponsored workers.
  5. Look at the Personal column for people with gaps.
  6. Note what you changed. A register that is kept up is a better answer than one that was tidied the night before.

What the register does not do

It is worth being plain about the limits.

  • It records and reminds. DBS and right to work rules are the employer's responsibility, and the register does not carry out checks.
  • It is for admins only. Staff do not see it and cannot upload their own documents.
  • It does not book holiday.
  • It is on the Enterprise plan.
  • It does not predict or promise an inspection outcome.

Try it on your own staff list

If your staff documents are spread across drives, files and diaries, begin with the people whose documents are closest to expiring. Our workforce compliance register page shows the screens, and the page on credential uploads and expiry alerts explains how the alerts work. You can try CareStream free for 14 days on a paid plan, and the Enterprise plan includes the register.

Start with one question from this post, the one you would least like to be asked, and see how quickly you can answer it with the document in your hand.

faqs.question: What is a DBS tracker?
faqs.answer: A DBS tracker is a record of each member of staff's Disclosure and Barring Service check: the certificate number, the date it was issued and any date you have set to look at it again. A good one also keeps the document itself and warns you in good time. CareStream's workforce compliance register does this for DBS and for the other documents a service holds on its staff.

faqs.question: How often does a DBS check need to be renewed?
faqs.answer: There is no single legal renewal date for a DBS certificate. Employers set their own review period in their recruitment policy, and many services use the DBS Update Service. Our guide on how often a DBS should be renewed goes through the options. In CareStream you record the date you want to be reminded and the register warns you 30 days before it.

faqs.question: Who is responsible for right to work checks?
faqs.answer: The employer. The GOV.UK employer's guide sets out how to carry out the checks, when to do follow up checks and which documents are acceptable. CareStream records the check, holds the document and reminds you when a time limit is coming up. It does not carry out the check for you.

faqs.question: Can we store NMC registration details in the same place?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the Enterprise plan. You choose the body (NMC, GPhC, HCPC, GMC, Social Work England or Other), record the registration number or PIN, upload the certificate and set the renewal or revalidation date. The register then treats it like any other expiring document.

faqs.question: What does an inspector expect to see in a staff file?
faqs.answer: Regulation 19 says certain information must be available for each person employed, and Schedule 3 lists it, including proof of identity with a recent photograph, the relevant criminal record certificate, evidence of conduct in previous employment, and a full employment history. What an inspector asks to see on the day is their call. A register helps you produce the document quickly. It does not decide the outcome.

faqs.question: Do staff see the register?
faqs.answer: No. The workforce register is for admins only. Staff do not see it, and the documents are not shown in the Staff Hub.

faqs.question: Which plan includes the workforce compliance register?
faqs.answer: The Enterprise plan. Check the pricing page for the current details.

title: Mobile Phone Policy in a Care Home: Safe Shared Tablets for Staff on the Floor
excerpt: Four beliefs stop care homes with a phone ban from using digital tools on the floor. Here is what is true about shared tablets, PINs and QR posters, and where the limits are.
meta_title: Mobile Phone Policy in a Care Home: Shared Tablets for Staff
meta_description: A care home with a phone ban still needs staff to reach policies, resident profiles and their own training. Here is what a safe shared tablet set up looks like.
content:
A carer on a night shift wants to check what the home's policy says about a resident who refuses medication. Her phone is in a locker, because the home has a ban on the floor. The policy folder is in the office, two corridors away.

That gap is where a mobile phone policy meets daily practice. Many homes keep the ban and add one or two tablets that everybody uses. It sounds simple, and it raises fair questions about security, records and who is doing what. Four beliefs come up again and again, so we take them one at a time.

Belief one: a phone ban means going back to paper

A ban on personal phones protects residents. It limits photographs, personal messaging during care and distraction on the floor. The ICO's data security guidance makes the point that organisations should control who can reach personal data and how. A mobile phone policy is one way a home does that.

But a ban does not remove the need to look things up. Staff still need the policy, the resident's preferences and their own training. If the only route is a folder in the office, the answer is often a guess.

A shared tablet is the middle route. It is the home's own equipment, kept in a staff area, which does a small number of jobs. In CareStream, a connected tablet shows nothing at all until a member of staff signs in. It opens on a Who's using it? screen, and nothing else is available without a personal PIN. Once a carer has signed in, they get their own hub, with Chat, the policy and guidance assistant, and This is me, the resident life story profiles.

Belief two: a shared tablet means a shared login

This is the one that worries managers most, and it is the one the design answers directly.

A shared login cannot tell you who did what. So the tablet itself holds no staff identity. It is a named tablet, for example Ward 2 tablet, set up by an administrator. It is not a staff member and does not count as a seat.

Every use is personal. Staff tap their picture or type their name under Who's using it?, then enter their own four digit PIN. They get their own full staff hub, exactly as on their own phone: Chat, This is me, their training and annual training, induction, actions, supervisions, follow ups, CQC questions, progress and records. The session goes back to the Who's using it? screen when they tap Done. After 4 minutes untouched a Still there? prompt appears, after 5 minutes untouched the session ends, and a session can run for 45 minutes of continuous use at most.

An administrator who enters their PIN on a tablet still gets an ordinary staff session. Admin screens can never be reached from a tablet. And because this is enforced by the server, not just hidden on the screen, a tablet cannot be used as a back door.

This is the practical difference between shared devices with one login and a shared tablet with personal PINs. The first hides people. The second keeps them identifiable.

Belief three: a QR code on the wall is a security hole

It is easy to see why. A code in a corridor sounds like an open door.

The poster works differently from a door key. The administrator prints a Connect a tablet poster from the Staff page. It shows the organisation logo from Settings and the CareStream logo. Scanning the QR code on the tablet opens a connect page. Nobody is signed in by the scan.

To connect, a member of staff:

  1. types the first letters of their name (no full staff list is shown before connecting)
  2. enters their own four digit PIN
  3. chooses which tablet it is

Wrong PIN guesses are limited per person and per poster, so a stranger cannot easily lock a colleague out, and cannot try endless guesses either. The poster is meant to be replaced regularly. In Settings, Shared tablets, an administrator chooses monthly, quarterly, half yearly or yearly reminders. Replacing the poster stops the old poster connecting new tablets. Tablets that are already connected stay connected.

If a tablet goes missing or leaves the building, the administrator can disconnect that tablet, or all of them, from the Staff page. It stops at once.

None of this makes a tablet impossible to misuse, and we do not claim it does. It means a connection needs a name and a personal PIN, is limited, and leaves a record.

Belief four: staff cannot do their own training without their own phone

Regulation 18 says staff must receive the support, training and professional development needed to do their work. For a home with a phone ban, the practical question is where the training happens.

With a tablet, staff do it in the home. They sign in with their PIN, open their own hub and see their training and actions, so a carer with 5 to 10 spare minutes can complete a lesson. Short lessons suit this setting, and our post on micro learning on a 12 hour shift looks at what works. For a night team, our piece on night shift policy access covers the same problem from the policy side.

Two honest points. First, the session ends after 5 minutes of no touch, with a Still there? prompt at 4 minutes, which is right for a shared screen. Second, the home decides when staff may use the tablet and whether it counts as paid time. That is a management decision, not a software one.

What a safe set up looks like

Whatever the product, a sound shared tablet arrangement tends to have the same features:

  • the tablet sits in a staff only area, not in a lounge or reception
  • nothing is visible without a personal sign in
  • each person can be identified in the record
  • there is a quick way to cut a tablet off
  • the connection method is replaced regularly
  • the home's written policy says what the tablet is for

On the Staff page, CareStream shows each tablet with a green dot when it is connected and when it was last used. Set up, connection and PIN events are recorded in an audit log. Every Chat question asked on a tablet is recorded against the person and the tablet, never anonymously.

How PINs are handled

A random four digit PIN is emailed to each staff member. It is shown as sent by the administrator, and administrators never see a PIN unless they choose Show PIN, which is logged. From the three dots menu on the Staff page an administrator can Re-send, Regenerate or Show a PIN, each limited to three an hour per person. Five wrong tries locks that person for five minutes. New staff receive their PIN with their welcome once the account has a tablet.

Agency workers are not listed on tablets, so they cannot use a tablet at all. Tablets never receive email or push notifications.

What shared tablets do not do

  • They do not replace your mobile phone policy. The provider remains responsible for its own policies, including what is allowed on the floor.
  • They do not decide data protection questions for you. CareStream records and controls access. Your information governance and data protection policies set the rules, and our policies on information governance and data protection are there to help you write them.
  • They do not make everything available. Without a PIN the tablet shows only the Who's using it? screen, and a signed in session shows that person's own hub.
  • They are not a rota, a handover record or a care record.
  • They are on paid plans only, up to five per account.

Setting one up this week

Start small. Choose one tablet and one place for it. Add it on the Staff page, print the poster, and ask three staff to connect it. Watch what they ask Chat for. Then look at This is me together, using the resident profiles you already hold. Our post on the This is me document explains what a good profile contains.

If you manage a home and want to see it working, the registered managers page shows how CareStream fits a manager's week, and the pricing page lists the plans that include shared tablets. You can book a demo and ask to see the Staff page and the poster.

faqs.question: Do we need a mobile phone policy if we have shared tablets?
faqs.answer: Yes. A shared tablet does not replace your own rules about personal phones. Your mobile phone policy says where phones may be kept, when they may be used and what happens with photographs. The tablet gives staff a work tool that fits that policy. Our care policy on social media, phones and photography is a starting point, and your provider decisions stay yours.

faqs.question: How many shared tablets can one care home have in CareStream?
faqs.answer: Up to five tablets per account on any paid plan. A tablet is not counted as a staff member or a seat. It is added on the Staff page with a name such as Ward 2 tablet and an optional location.

faqs.question: Can anyone who picks up the tablet see resident information?
faqs.answer: No. Before a PIN is entered, a connected tablet shows only a Who's using it? screen. There is no open Chat and no open This is me. A member of staff types their name or taps their picture and enters their own four digit PIN, and then sees their own hub. Every Chat question is recorded against the person and the tablet. The session ends after 5 minutes untouched, with a Still there? prompt at 4 minutes, and the tablet should still live in a staff area.

faqs.question: What stops a stranger connecting a tablet with the QR code?
faqs.answer: The QR code on the poster signs nobody in. To connect a tablet, a member of staff types the first letters of their name, enters their own four digit PIN and chooses which tablet it is. Wrong guesses are limited per person and per poster. Replacing the poster stops the old one connecting new tablets.

faqs.question: What happens if a PIN is forgotten?
faqs.answer: An administrator can Re-send the same PIN, Regenerate a new one, or choose Show PIN, which is logged. These are in the three dots menu on the Staff page. Each is limited to three an hour per person. Five wrong tries locks that person for five minutes.

faqs.question: Are agency workers on the tablet?
faqs.answer: No. Agency workers are not listed on tablets, so they cannot use a tablet at all.

faqs.question: Does the tablet get emails or push notifications?
faqs.answer: No. Tablets never receive email or push notifications. PINs are emailed to staff, not to the tablet.
